name: Kansas

regions.name: Rolling Plains and Breaks / Central Rolling Red Plains (Western-Central)

context: K-State MF2206: February through May is the critical wind erosion period in Kansas, but soil can blow any time high winds hit smooth, wide fields with little cover; fall-planted fields are most at risk after drought or crop failure, and burning or removing residue for forage is a serious hazard.

MF2206 Table 1: at most western and central stations erosive winds come from the north (0°, or 338° at Goodland and Hill City) in winter and early spring and from the south (158-202°) from about April-May into October; Chanute, Fort Riley and Olathe are mostly southerly all year. Emergency tillage in most of Kansas runs east-west.
The WEQ climatic factor C is scaled to Garden City, Kansas (C = 100). Kansas plans for 329, 345, 588 and 609 use WEPS runs to set residue amounts, ridge direction and critical periods.

Kansas NRCS uses Western, Central and Eastern seeding zones drawn on county lines (Western ends at Norton-Graham-Trego-Ness-Hodgeman-Ford-Clark; Eastern starts at Washington-Clay-Dickinson-Marion-Butler-Cowley); grass shares, fertilizer and seedbed rules differ by zone.

Kansas law (K.S.A. 2-2001 to 2-2009) requires stopping soil blowing that damages land downwind or public health; county commissioners may order emergency control and assess the land, capped at $3 per acre per year unless that does not cover the cost (MF2206).

KS 550/512/327: a standing cover crop or surface mulch is required for grass seedings in MLRAs 72, 73, 74, 75, 77, 78, 79 and 80A; clean-tilled seedbeds are allowed only in MLRAs 76, 84A, 106, 107B, 112 and 116B where erosion or moisture is not a concern (TN KS-PM-31).

KS Agronomy TN-47: flex-fallow is meant mainly for Kansas west of the 24-inch rainfall belt; fallow often stores no more than 30% of fallow-season rain, and Garden City research found growing a crop in place of fallow cut wheat and sorghum yields in dry years.
Forestry TN KS-10: soil blowing is a concern on sandy and organic wet soils (suitability group 2), and blowing-soil abrasion is a main limit for tree plantings on sandy groups 5 and 7.
cover_rules: KS 340 soil health: mixes of at least 3 species; for organic matter at least 5 species incl. a legume with C:N above 30; aim for 80-100% ground cover. Plan ≥325,000 seeds/ac in Zone 1 (far west), 450,000 in Zone 2 (next band east), 650,000 in Zone 3 (central and east).
KS 340: where wind erosion is a concern, cover crops in rows wider than 20 in must run perpendicular to the prevailing wind during the critical wind erosion period; drilling is preferred.

KS 340 aerial or last-pass seeding: raise the rate 1.5 times and sow 7-10 days earlier than drilled covers. Brassicas need about 4 weeks before the average 28°F freeze and soil >45°F; sorghum-sudan and millet need soil >65°F; aerial-seed clovers before Sep 5.

KS 340/550: rye or rye hybrids are not approved as the cover ahead of a permanent grass seeding (allelopathy). In soil-health covers rye may be used but should be dead about 14 days before the cash crop is planted.

KS 340: keep buckwheat out of fields in rotation with or within 30 ft of commodity wheat, and grow no commodity wheat for 2 calendar years after it; review K-State MF2866 (Hessian fly) before using rye, barley or other wheat relatives.

KS Agronomy TN-47 flex-fallow: replace fallow with a cover crop only when a Paul Brown probe goes ≥12 in (preferably >18 in) into moist soil and the CPC outlook through wheat planting is neutral or wetter; otherwise leave the field fallow.

K-State MF3523: post-wheat covers in the High Plains could not be grazed about half the time; with about 1,000 lb/ac or less of forage, skip grazing if soil protection is the goal, keeping ≥30% ground cover (~1,000 lb/ac). Control volunteer wheat (wheat streak mosaic).

KS 340: haying or chopping a soil-health cover is not allowed; the standard notes most covers reach about 90% canopy plus surface cover and ≥4,000 lb/ac dry biomass, and the dust purpose needs ≥80% ground cover kept during planting of the next crop.
residue: KS 345: in wind erosion areas keep at least 1,000 lb/ac of flat small-grain residue equivalent on the surface throughout the critical wind erosion period unless the KS 345 implementation requirements (WEPS-based) set otherwise; choose crops from Table 5 that tolerate blowing soil.

KS 329/345: follow fragile-residue crops (soybeans, sunflowers, canola, dry beans, fall-seeded covers) with nonfragile ones (wheat, sorghum, corn, millet) and low-residue with high-residue crops; never grow fragile low-residue crops more than 2 years in a row.

KS 329 no-till: annual STIR no more than 10 for no-till seeding, 15 for strip-till, 20 for direct seed; rotary harrows and vertical tillage tools count as full-width tillage (345). Combines must spread small-grain straw over about 80% of header width.

KS 329/345 snow catch: leave stubble ≥10 in tall for rows under 15 in and ≥15 in for wider rows over at least 50% of the field; shred stalks only after the main snowfall period; limit fall tillage to undercutting blades or sweeps or deep rippers that keep stubble standing (345).
KS 345 for moisture: keep at least 2,000 lb/ac or 70% residue cover all year. Residue produced: winter wheat 102 lb per bu, corn and grain sorghum 56 lb per bu; fall wheat growth adds 175-400 lb/ac.

KS 345 Table 3, nonfragile residue left per pass: moldboard plow 0-10%, offset or tandem disk 25-70%, chisel with twisted shovels 35-70%, sweep plow wider than 30 in 75-95%, no-till drill with smooth coulters in standing stubble 85-95%.
KS 329/345: no residue burning; haying or grazing residue is limited to what still meets the planned objectives, and KS 528 does not allow crop-residue use below the planned minimum.
KS 329/345: small-grain straw cut fine by a combine straw chopper counts as fragile residue when estimating cover.
barriers: KS 603 herbaceous wind barriers: stiff, erect, lodging-resistant plants at least 1.5 ft tall with 40-50% porosity during the erosion period; rows within a barrier ≤36 in apart; barriers spaced no more than 10 times their height (±10% for equipment).

KS 603: replant annual barriers every year and fill gaps (e.g., 10-15 ft) quickly; move or rebuild barriers that fill with sediment or pond runoff; orient them to handle water flow where water erosion also occurs.
KS 603 guidance (PM TN KS-1) lists approved varieties by MLRA; for example tall wheatgrass 'Jose' and switchgrass 'Blackwell' are rated adapted in every Kansas MLRA.

KS 585 wind stripcropping: strips at 65-90° to the prevailing erosive wind; protective strips at least as wide as erodible strips and never under 25 ft; narrow strips of tall wind-tolerant crops may protect sensitive crops if spaced no more than 20 times their height.
KS 386 field border for wind: put it on the windward field edge, at least 30 ft wide, with stiff upright grasses or forbs at least 1 ft tall during the critical wind erosion period.
KS CRP TG-22: CP24 cross wind trap strips are permanent cover strips perpendicular to the prevailing wind on cropland with a wind erodibility index (EI) of 4 or more; not allowed on terraces.

KS 588 cross wind ridges: within 45° of perpendicular to the erosive wind in the critical period, ridge spacing ≤4 times ridge height; suited to loamy and clayey soils, poorly suited to sands, and on sandy loams build them only when moist.
windbreak: KS 380 PS: the most effective belt has 5 rows at right angles to the wind: 1-2 shrub rows windward, tall trees in the center, at least one evergreen row toward the leeward side, fruit-bearing plants leeward of the evergreens. Put primary belts north and west of what they protect.

KS 380 for wind erosion: average density 50% in the erosion season (spring, when hardwoods are leafless), so include a conifer or dense shrub row; protection reaches 10H leeward and 2H windward; field belts usually 10H-20H apart. Use other practices until it works (≤20 yr).

KS 380 spacing (in row / between rows, ft): shrubs under 10 ft 3-6 / 12-30; pines and junipers 8-16 / 12-30; small trees 10-25 ft tall 8-16 / 12-30; trees over 25 ft 8-25 / 12-30; rows ≥4 ft wider than maintenance equipment, at least 12 ft.

KS 380 siting: windward rows ≥200 ft from road centerline on the north or west side, ≥80 ft on the south or east; fireguards ≥8 ft from driplines; exclude livestock; keep other rows 25 ft from cottonwood, silver maple, honeylocust or hybrid willow.

KS 380: except for eastern redcedar and Rocky Mountain juniper, no more than 2 rows of one species; consider ≥2 conifer rows in multi-row belts. Rocky Mountain juniper is not recommended in MLRAs 75, 76, 84A, 106, 107, 112; both junipers host cedar-apple rust.

KS-ECS-9: plant bareroot and containerized stock after frost leaves the ground and no later than May 1; containerized also Sep 15-Oct 30 with good moisture. On erosive sites till only narrow strips (4-5 ft; 10 ft with fabric) or seed oats or spring grain early enough to reach 4-6 in before freeze-up.

KS-ECS-9 between-row grass: blue grama 2, buffalograss 5, sideoats grama 6 or little bluestem 4 lb PLS/ac (pure stand), with a 4-ft weed-free zone around each tree for 3 years; never smooth brome or fescue between rows.

Forestry TN KS-10: on sandy suitability group 5, weed competition and blowing-soil abrasion are the main limits; on group 7 sands, drought and abrasion; group 7 hummocky sands need special site preparation, undisturbed vegetation between rows, and often supplemental water or weed fabric.
roughening: KS 609: surface roughening is emergency tillage only, not a primary control; it must cut predicted erosion by 25%. Start on the windward edge as soon as blowing begins or cover is clearly short, working at right angles to the wind.

KS 609 PS chisels: points 2-4 ft apart on sandy or pulverized soils, 2-6 ft on loams and clays, 5-6 ft in a growing crop; remove harrows. Listers or downward-pitched shovels: ridges 4-8 in high and 16-32 in wide; re-furrow if drifting soil fills them.
KS 609 PS heavy tools: subsoil rippers making ridges ≥4 in high spaced 6-30 ft; a road grader with a steep blade angle can throw ridges 14 in high with furrows about 18 in deep, 10-30 ft apart.

KS 609 Table 1: loose dry sand—list or build large ridges; frozen soil—chisel or rip; dry loam-clay, cloddy or pulverized—list; thin drifting layer over firm moist loam-clay—chisel; winter cereals on frozen soil—chisel or rip.

K-State MF2206 sands: clods will not hold, so build ridges: 14-in moldboard lister 40-50 in apart (or 8-in lister on 20-24 in), first pass no deeper than about 4-5 in, later passes deeper or split the ridge; manure on the ridges helps.

MF2206 clays: 2-in chisel on 24-54 in spacing, 3-6 in deep; loams: 4-in shovels, closer where bare. Tilling every other pass (50%) works with 20-24 in chisel spacing; if blowing continues, till the skipped strips or split the spacing deeper.

MF2206: 2-3 mph makes the largest, most durable clods (use ahead of a forecast blow); 5-7 mph makes the roughest surface (use once soil is moving). Watch for dry high-wind days (>25 mph) and test tillage beforehand.

MF2206 in growing wheat: 40-in chisel spacing 4-6 in deep cut yield 5.5 bu/ac on the shank rows but about 1 bu/ac field-wide; check crop insurance first. Mulch option: 1.5-2 t/ac straw or hay, 3-4 t/ac stover or 15-20 t/ac wet manure, anchored.
grazing: KS 528 range: use no more than 50% by weight of the key species' current growth in the growing season, and no more than 65% if grazed while dormant (with ≤50% taken while growing). Warm-season growing season is May 1-Oct 31.
KS 528 dormant-season residual (instead of utilization): shortgrass 300-500 lb/ac, midgrass 750-1,000 lb/ac, tallgrass 1,200-1,500 lb/ac.

KS 528 Table 7 heights (begin / stop / regrowth by frost): native tallgrasses 8-16 / 4 / 8 in; little bluestem and sideoats 6-10 / 4 / 6 in; buffalograss and blue grama 4-6 / 2 / 4 in; leave 1-2 in more under continuous grazing.
KS 528 recovery for native forage: 25-45 days in rapid growth, 45-60 moderate, 60-90 slow; use the long end in low-rainfall areas; start the rotation in a different unit each year.
KS 528 starting harvest efficiency on range: continuous grazing 25% growing + 7.5% dormant = 32.5% a year; 8 or more pastures 30% + 9% = 39%.
KS 528 to rebuild vigor: hold use of key species to 30-40%, or rest at least 60 days up to a full year, giving priority to rest at green-up or just before dormancy.

KS 528 erosion: keep areas of animal concentration under 10% of a grazing unit; set cover or residue targets from erosion tools; place feed and supplement sites so cattle do not trail on steep or erosive soils.
drought: K-State MF3716 (west of Russell and the 99th meridian): April+May+June rain predicts forage. Below 75% of average, forage drops by about the same percentage; at 75% or more, yield was ≥90% of average 90% of the time.

MF3716 turnout: last year stressed and soil dry in March-early April—delay 2-4 weeks (grass 3-4 in) and/or cut stocking 15-25%; stressed but moist—delay ≤2 weeks and/or cut 10-15%; unstressed but dry—delay or cut up to 10%.
MF3716 mid-season: if Apr-Jun rain is under 75% of average, cut stocking a further 10-15% (unstressed start) or 15-20% (stressed start), or by the rain deficit percentage.

MF3716 (Hays) heights at 50% use by mid-August: big bluestem 5.0 in, little bluestem 4.0, blue grama 3.8, sideoats 3.7, buffalograss 2.0, western wheatgrass 10.0; pastures shorter than this may enter next year stressed.

MF3716: keep leaf removal at or below 50%; removing 70% stops growth of well over half the roots for 17 days and 90% stops all root growth for 17 days. If dry years continue two or more years, plant growth, tiller density and even survival can suffer.
MF3716 relief: wean early, pregnancy-check and cull opens early, cull poor performers, sell stockers first, or move cattle to drylot or leased pasture outside the drought area.

KS 528: every grazing plan needs a written contingency plan with drought triggers; when conditions are not right for grazing, follow it rather than graze (the spec points to the National Drought Mitigation Center and GRASSCAST).

MF2206: winter wheat and other fall-planted fields can blow during low cover in winter and early spring, especially after a drought year or crop failure; scout and mulch or roughen before soil starts moving.
seeding: KS 550/512/327: standing cover or mulch required in MLRAs 72-75, 77-79, 80A. Sorghum stubble at seeding 1,750 lb/ac (I ≤56), 2,000 (I 86), 2,250 (I 134 or ≥220); small-grain 1,500 lb/ac flat equivalent, not allowed where I >86. Add mulch to reach these.

KS 550: keep cover-crop stubble at least 12 in tall and stop it setting seed; growing wheat can be the seedbed only if grazed out by May 1; no inversion tillage in surface-mulch seedbeds; firm loose soil so a shoe sinks no more than ½ in.

TN KS-PM-31 drilling: drill with ≤10-in rows, double-disk openers preferred, depth control and press wheels; seed ⅛-½ in deep (eastern gamagrass 1 in; Indian ricegrass ½-1 in, 1-3 in on coarse soils). Broadcast only on small areas, covering ⅛-½ in.

KS 550 mixes: ≥5 grasses within zone percent limits; forbs and legumes ≤1 bulk lb or ½ PLS lb/ac in all, ≤¼ bulk lb each, Maximilian sunflower ≤1/10 bulk lb; introduced legumes ≤10% each and ≤20% total; species rate = full rate × share.

TN KS-PM-31 seed origin: named varieties from PM TN KS-1; otherwise native-harvest seed from within 400 mi south or 150 mi north and ≤1,500 ft higher, traced to state and county. A Kansas germination test is valid 9 months (5 if shipped interstate).

KS 550 establishment: do not graze native seedlings the first year (flash grazing for weeds allowed); spray when weeds exceed 50% canopy; mow above seedlings, not at >95°F with <30% humidity, and generally not after July 15.
TN KS-PM-31: native stands are not judged failed until the 2nd-3rd season; more than 2.0 plants per 1.92-ft² frame is acceptable, 0.5-2.0 questionable, under 0.5 a failure.

TN KS-PM-31: NRCS will not plan a seeding to convert never-tilled native rangeland; adding species there needs specialist approval, only plants listed in the ecological site description, and no tillage.
dont_seed: K.A.R. 4-8-44 (amended May 15, 2026) noxious weeds: hoary cress, leafy spurge, quackgrass, Russian knapweed, kudzu, spotted and diffuse knapweed (A); Canada thistle, common and cutleaf teasel (B); field bindweed, musk thistle, sericea lespedeza, Johnsongrass, bur ragweed, Amur honeysuckle (C).
KS 340: seed must meet the Kansas Noxious Weed Law and Seed Law with weed seed ≤0.5%; species not in the KS tables may make up ≤20% of a mix and must not be locally invasive.

Range TN KS-11: Caucasian bluestem and yellow (plains) bluestem, Johnsongrass and sericea lespedeza are remove-only grassland pests; its prevention list says not to plant pest species that can invade grassland.

Range TN KS-11: smooth brome and tall fescue are pests in native rangeland (not always in managed pasture). KS 342: tall fescue is not approved and smooth brome is limited to 50% in the Western seeding zone.
KS 550/340: no cereal rye or rye hybrids as the cover ahead of a perennial grass seeding (allelopathy); no buckwheat in or within 30 ft of commodity wheat.
KS 550 Table 2: introduced legumes ≤10% each and ≤20% together; Maximilian sunflower ≤5% of a mix; CRP TG-75 advises holding yellow or white sweetclover to ≤10%.

Range TN KS-11 woody remove-only pests: Siberian elm, Russian olive, saltcedar, Callery pear, black locust, white mulberry, autumn olive, multiflora rose and Amur, Tatarian, Morrow's and Japanese honeysuckle; TN KS-10 warns Freedom honeysuckle can turn invasive.
pasture: KS 512 full rates (PLS lb/ac): smooth brome 10-12, tall fescue 12-15, intermediate wheatgrass 12-15, meadow brome 12-16, orchardgrass 3-4, western wheatgrass 10-12, bermudagrass seed 3-5 (sprigs 15-20 bu), switchgrass 5-6, big bluestem or indiangrass 8-10; alfalfa 6-8.

KS 512 dates (statewide, +2 weeks allowed): warm-season grasses Dec 1-May 15; cool-season grasses and legumes Dec 1-Apr 15 and Aug 15-Oct 1; sprigs Mar 1-May 15. Use species rated 7 or higher in the MLRA forage suitability group.

KS 528 introduced forage heights (begin / stop / by frost): bermudagrass 4-8 / 3 / 6 in; smooth or meadow brome 6-10 / 3 / 6; tall fescue 5-7 / 3 / 4; sorghum-sudan and pearl millet 18-36 / 8 in; wheat or rye pasture 6-8 / 4 in.

KS 511 hay: native prairie, big bluestem and indiangrass one cutting before July 20 at boot to medium head, cut no lower than 4 in, 8 in regrowth by frost; bermudagrass and brome cut at 3 in, 6 in by frost; tall fescue 3 in, 4 in by frost.
KS 528 pasture harvest efficiency: continuous 30% growing + 9% dormant = 39%; 8 or more paddocks 35% + 10.5% = 45.5%. Tame-forage recovery: 14-25 days rapid growth, 25-30 moderate, 30-50 slow.
KS 528: where Pasture Condition Score indicators are 3 or less, raise stop heights 1-2 in or rest at least 30 days (up to half a season), favoring rest at green-up or before dormancy.
KS 511 and K-State MF3523: sorghums, sudangrass and Johnsongrass carry nitrate and prussic-acid risk; test stressed annual forage before grazing and take care grazing sorghums after frost.
crp: Kansas CRP supplement: no management or maintenance during the primary nesting season Apr 15-Jul 15 once cover is established; no cosmetic mowing, travel lanes, or bale and machinery storage.

CRP haying (KS 511): only after the cover is established and once in any 3-year period, between Jul 15 and Aug 31; cut no lower than 5 in, leave 25% unharvested and 20 ft by water; remove bales within 15 days.

CRP grazing (KS 528): no more than 120 days, not past Nov 1, and remove stock when average cover height reaches 5 in; 50% of carrying capacity if grazed in nesting season; no grazing within 20 ft of water.
KS CRP TG-62 managed or emergency use: take no more than 50% of current growth by weight and graze no lower than an average 5-in stubble; cut native hay once, soon after Jul 15, at 5 in or higher.

Kansas CRP: out of compliance once tree height exceeds grass height and tree canopy reaches 1%; CP2 and CP4D may carry up to 10% shrub canopy; maintain enrolled practices for the life of the contract and control noxious weeds as State law requires.
KS CRP TG-53 light disking: no deeper than 3 in, leave at least 25% of the grass alive, only after fall dormancy and before Apr 15.

Expiring CRP (K-State MF2827): killing grass with herbicide and no-till or reduced-till planting is often cheapest; keep buffers or contour grass strips on erodible spots; expect higher N needs for 2 years; leaving it in grass keeps wind and water protection.

Reseeding failed stands on loose sand (Range TN KS-6): no tillage; drill into weed stubble or a standing cover ≤½ in deep with light opener pressure; weed control is mandatory the first 60 days; mow mid-summer leaving stubble to cut sandblasting.
disturbed: KS 342: seed in the normal windows (cool-season Aug 15-Oct 1 or Dec 1-Apr 15; warm-season Dec 1-May 15) or, when waiting is impractical, right after construction; mulch per KS 484 immediately where erosion is a concern.
KS 342: shape first; salvage topsoil and respread in ≤6-in lifts after ripping the graded subsoil; till 3 in across the slope and firm until a footprint is ≤⅛ in deep; drill ¼-¾ in deep.

KS 342 fertilizer without a soil test (lb/ac): Western N 20-30; Central N 30-40, P2O5 40-60; Eastern N 40-50, P2O5 60-80; no nitrogen when seeding only natives. One ton of manure ≈ 10 lb N, 5 P2O5, 10 K2O.

KS Urban TN KS-1 temporary cover (<1 yr): oats 80-110, wheat or rye 60-120, barley 50-100, annual ryegrass 5-10 lb/ac drilled (Feb 15-May 15 or Aug 1-Sep 15/Oct 15); sorghum-sudan 35 lb/ac May 15-Jul 1; 50 lb/ac N-P-K where rain is under 30 in.
KS 484: straw or hay mulch must give at least 70% ground cover, anchored by crimping, tackifier or netting if needed to hold it in place; wood mulch ≥2 in deep; gravel pieces ≥0.75 in, 2 in deep.

KS 342 Table 4 critical-area rates (PLS lb/ac): sideoats grama 12, switchgrass 6, western wheatgrass 20, little bluestem 8, blue grama 3, buffalograss 8, tall wheatgrass 20 on saline spots; Western zone allows brome ≤50% and no tall fescue.

KCC K.A.R. 82-3-602: close drilling and haul-off pits within 365 days after spud and work-over pits within 90 days after work-over ends; on abandoning a pit, grade the surface and return it as nearly as practicable to its prior condition.

PM TN KS-26 brine scars: test EC, ESP and pH; add straw, hay, manure or wood chips to help leach salts, gypsum for sodic soils; only tall wheatgrass, Russian wildrye and western wheatgrass established consistently (Graham Co. study); mulch 3-5 t/ac crimped, no grazing until established.
dunes: KS 342 dunes and blowouts: fence blowouts larger than about 2 acres when the pasture is grazed in the growing season, setting the fence back from the edges; not needed if ungrazed or winter-only; natural recovery under protection is allowed where good grasses remain.

KS 342: prepare blowouts with a cover crop, or natural mulch or manure, then seed sand bluestem 10-30%, prairie sandreed 20-30%, switchgrass 10-30%, little bluestem 10-20%, sand lovegrass 10-20% (full rates 12, 8, 6, 8, 2 PLS lb/ac); forbs ≤1 PLS lb/ac extra.

KS CRP TG-84 sandy sites: forage sorghum 10-12 lb/ac on 10-12 in rows by May 31 with ≥12 in net irrigation Jun-Aug; mulch thin spots and hilltops (manure ≥30 t/ac); no-till native seed Dec 1-May 15; 0.5 plants per frame counts as established.
PM TN KS-28 (western Kansas sands): an irrigated sorghum cover needed about 5-9.5 in to reach full cover; first-year native grass 5-13.25 in, and year two 8.25-21.75 in.

Kansas Choppy Sands range site (MLRA 72, 77): with overgrazing, sand bluestem, switchgrass, little bluestem and prairie sandreed decline, the fine sand begins to blow, and active dunes and blowouts form—keep a good vegetative cover.
MF2206: on loose sand clods will not hold, so use listers: a 14-in lister 40-50 in apart or 8-in on 20-24 in, a shallow first pass (about 4-5 in), then deeper or split ridges.
KS 588: cross wind ridges are poorly suited to sands; on very fine sandy loams to sands build them only when moist, because they break down quickly.
notes: Manhattan PMC releases with listed commercial seed vendors (PM TN KS-30, 2011): Kaw big bluestem, Chet and Garden sand bluestem, El Reno sideoats, Texoka buffalograss, Pronghorn prairie sandreed, Bend sand lovegrass, Blackwell and Kanlow switchgrass, Barton western wheatgrass, Aldous and Cimarron little bluestem, Cheyenne and Osage indiangrass.

Manhattan PMC forb releases (TN KS-30): Riley partridge pea, Kaneb purple prairieclover, Reno Illinois bundleflower, Prairie Gold Maximilian sunflower, Midas false sunflower, Kanoka roundhead lespedeza, Eureka thickspike gayfeather, Sunglow coneflower, Nekan pitcher sage; also Pete and Verl gamagrass.

KS 340 table rates as Excellent erosion fighters: annual ryegrass, winter barley, cereal rye, winter wheat, spring and winter triticale, forage sorghum, sorghum-sudangrass, pearl millet; oats, corn and most millets rate Very Good; brassicas Good (hybrid forage turnip Very Good); flax, sunflower and safflower Fair.

Kansas Forest Service seedlings: evergreens (eastern redcedar, eastern white pine, oriental arborvitae, ponderosa pine, Rocky Mountain juniper, southwestern white pine); shrubs (American and sandhill plum, caragana, chokecherry, elderberry, fragrant sumac, golden currant, lilac, ninebark, Peking cotoneaster).

Kansas Forest Service deciduous seedlings include bur, chinkapin, English, northern red and Shumard oak, hackberry, honeylocust, cottonwood, black walnut, pecan, sycamore, baldcypress, persimmon, pawpaw, redbud and silver maple; used in inner windbreak rows for height.

KS 380 renovation: release sod-bound belts with at least 70% stand by herbicide or shallow (≤3 in) cultivation no closer than 1 ft to trees; root-prune 18-24 in deep at or beyond the drip line every 5-10 years; cut leggy shrubs to 4-8 in when dormant.

CRP pollinator mixes (KS CRP TG-75/77): Central and Eastern mixes should carry 18-20 species, with at least 10 forbs and legumes including 3 starting to bloom in May, 3 in Jun-Aug and 3 in Sep; the Western example mix is acceptable statewide.

Region mapping caveat: MLRA 73 and 78C straddle the Western and Central seeding zones and parts of 74 and 75 lie in the Eastern zone; Kansas zone rules are county-based, so the MLRA grouping is an approximation (TN KS-PM-31 App. B).

cover.name: Oats
cover.rate: 40-60 lb/ac, rows ≤20 in, as cover before grass seeding; temporary cover 80-110 lb/ac drilled (110-140 broadcast)
cover.note: Plant Aug 1-Sep 15 ahead of a spring perennial seeding; usually winter-kills; if it survives, kill at 5th-6th leaf to boot before the seeded grass emerges.

cover.name: Winter wheat
cover.rate: 40-60 lb/ac, rows ≤20 in, before grass seeding; temporary cover 60-120 lb/ac drilled (60-125 broadcast)
cover.note: Kill at 5th-6th leaf to boot, or seed grass into growing wheat grazed out by May 1. Rated Excellent erosion fighter in the KS 340 table.

cover.name: Cereal rye
cover.note: Excellent erosion fighter, but not approved as a cover before perennial seedings (allelopathic); in soil-health covers terminate about 14 days before seeding the cash crop.

cover.name: Barley
cover.note: Temporary cover Feb 15-May 15 or Aug 1-Oct 15; winter barley rated Excellent erosion fighter, spring barley Good.

cover.name: Triticale
cover.rate: 80 lb/ac as temporary cover on acid reshaped sites (rye, triticale or oats); 20 lb/ac in K-State post-wheat grazing mixes
cover.note: Overwinters for later fall and spring grazing; rated Excellent erosion fighter.

cover.name: Forage sorghum / sudangrass
cover.rate: 6-12 lb/ac, rows ≤20 in (40-in rows allowed on sands in MLRA 72, 73, 77, 78, 79); 10-12 lb/ac on 10-12 in rows on CREP sandy sites
cover.note: Plant the summer before grass seeding, no later than Aug 1; leave ≥12 in stubble and the KS 550 residue minimum. Nitrate and prussic acid risk if grazed.

cover.name: Grain sorghum (milo)
cover.note: Standing stubble seedbed for grass; male-sterile hybrids or late planting limit seed set.

cover.name: Sorghum-sudangrass (temporary cover)
cover.note: May 15-Jul 1 on disturbed or construction sites needing cover for less than a year.

cover.name: Annual ryegrass
cover.note: Feb 15-May 15 or Aug 1-Sep 15; aerial seeding needs 2-3 lb/ac more than drilling.

cover.name: Post-wheat grazing cover mix (K-State)
cover.rate: per acre: triticale 20 lb, Austrian winter pea 4-6, sorghum-sudan 4, cowpea 4-5, sunflower 1-3, millet 2, radish 1, rapeseed 0.5, phacelia 0.2 lb (sunn hemp 0.75 lb in 2018)
cover.note: High Plains on-farm mixes planted July 7-20 (one Sep 11) in 2017-18; sorghum-sudan or millet gave 55-80% of yield when there was enough forage to graze.

cover.name: Multispecies cover mix example 1 (C:N about 43), sandy CREP sites
cover.rate: oats 25 + lentils 5 + rapeseed 2 + flax 5 + safflower 5 = 42 lb/ac (1,275,000 seeds/ac)
cover.note: KS CRP TG-84 example; goal of 5+ species with a legume, C:N >35, ≥1,000,000 seeds/ac and 80-100% cover.

cover.name: Multispecies cover mix example 3 (C:N about 35), sandy CREP sites
cover.rate: soybean 1 + cowpea 3 + crimson clover 1 + sudangrass 9 + pearl millet 5 + rapeseed 1 + sunflower 2 + flax 1 = 23 lb/ac (1,071,300 seeds/ac)
cover.note: KS CRP TG-84 example; stack spring, summer and fall covers within a year if one does not reach 80% cover.

coverPlant.text: Oats as standing cover for a spring grass seeding: plant Aug 1-Sep 15 at 40-60 lb/ac (TN KS-PM-31 App. A).
Fall temporary cover: wheat, barley or rye Aug 1-Oct 15; oats and annual ryegrass Aug 1-Sep 15 (Urban TN KS-1).
Spring temporary cover: oats, wheat, barley, rye or annual ryegrass Feb 15-May 15 (Urban TN KS-1).
Summer sorghum covers: sorghum-sudan May 15-Jul 1 for temporary cover; forage or grain sorghum standing cover planted the summer before grass seeding, no later than Aug 1.
High Plains post-wheat covers: plant Jul 10-Aug 10, after wheat harvest when moisture allows; start grazing Oct 10-Jan 30 and end 30-60 days later (K-State MF3523).
Irrigated sandy sites in western Kansas: plant forage sorghum cover on 10-12 in rows no later than May 31, irrigating ≥12 in net Jun-Aug (CRP TG-84; PM TN KS-28).

seedWin.text: Warm-season native grass, optimum Mar 15-May 15 (planner may extend 2 weeks).
Warm-season grass alternate (dormant) window Dec 1-May 15; sandy CREP sites should seed early in it to use winter and spring moisture.
Cool-season grasses and legumes, drilled: optimum Aug 15-Oct 1; a small-grain nurse crop may be added (oats Aug-mid Sep, wheat late Sep, 20-30 lb/ac).
Cool-season grasses and legumes, alternate Dec 1-Apr 15 (no nurse crop with spring seedings).
Native forbs and legumes: optimum Mar 15-Apr 15; alternate Dec 1-May 15.
Frost-seeding introduced legumes, Eastern zone only: Nov 1-Dec 31 optimum, to Feb 15 alternate; broadcast 2 PLS lb/ac.
Bermudagrass sprigs Mar 1-May 15 (15-day extension possible); varieties are adapted south of the Smoky Hill/Kansas rivers and not in MLRA 72, 77, 106, 107.
Reseeding failed native seedings: preferred Mar 20-Apr 30, acceptable Feb 1-May 15 (introduced: Aug 15-Oct 1 preferred).
Brine-damaged saline sites: seed cool-season grasses as a late-fall dormant seeding, in winter or very early spring, when surface salinity is lowest.
Trees and shrubs: bareroot and containerized after frost leaves the ground, no later than May 1; containerized also Sep 15-Oct 30.

mixes.title: KS 550 example mix: Loamy Upland, Eastern seeding zone
mixes.note: Total 5.6 PLS lb/ac (30/25/15/10/10/10% of full rates). Forbs may be added up to ½ PLS lb/ac without cutting grass rates. Same example in TN KS-PM-31 Table 6.

mixes.title: KS CRP TG-84 example mix for sandy CREP sites
mixes.note: Source gives % of mix and full PLS rates; rows here = full rate × share (KS 550 method), total about 4.29. Add at least 1 lb/ac of forbs and shrubs (example: fourwing saltbush 0.2, winterfat 0.1, alfalfa and Maximilian sunflower 0.1 each). No-till into existing cover.

species: Rocky Mountain juniper (conifer, Western zone only)
Oriental arborvitae (conifer, Eastern and Central zones)
Hackberry (tall tree; Western zone only on group 1 soils)
Eastern cottonwood (tall tree, moist group 1-2 soils)
Fourwing saltbush (shrub; Western zone, or saline group 9 soils in all zones)
avoid: Osage orange or honeylocust beside native range (remove-only grassland pests)
Eastern redcedar or Rocky Mountain juniper in commercial apple areas (cedar-apple rust)
Smooth brome or tall fescue between tree rows

shrubs.name: Eastern redcedar
advice: KS 314 Table 1: canopy over 15% is a high infestation, 6-15% medium, under 5% low; listed methods are cutting below green growth, prescribed fire (controls it), and soil-applied herbicide.
KS 314: burning is most effective and cheapest before brush reaches the medium level and 5 ft height; repeated annual burns may be needed, with grazing adjusted to build fine fuel.

Range TN KS-11: eastern redcedar is a remove-only grassland pest; treeless land within 200 yards of a mature tree is exposed to seed. Map recruits, remove seed trees and perches (old fences, dead trees) and burn at historic or higher frequency.
Kansas CRP: a field can be out of compliance once tree height exceeds grass height and tree canopy reaches 1%.

shrubs.name: Sand sagebrush
advice: KS 314 Table 1: over 30% canopy is high, 20-30% medium; mowing reduces it, fire reduces it, and foliar herbicide is the listed chemical.
Range TN KS-11 rates sand sagebrush a native remove/reduce/manipulate species: it is targeted for removal only where significant recruitment is occurring on the site.

KS 314: where erosion potential is high choose the method with the least soil disturbance and time mechanical work so bare soil is not exposed for long; on Choppy Sands range, overgrazing increases sand sagebrush and the fine sand can begin to blow into dunes and blowouts.
KS CRP TG-84 allows sand sagebrush at 0-0.1 lb/ac as a shrub in sandy-site CREP seed mixes.

shrubs.name: Honeylocust and Osage orange (hedge)
advice: KS 314 Table 1: over 15% canopy is high, 6-15% medium, under 5% low; cut and treat the cut surface; burning reduces them only with 2 or more yearly fires; foliar, soil or basal-bark herbicides.

KS 314 PS: do not bulldoze resprouting species such as honeylocust or hedge; cut-stump with herbicide applied right after cutting is the preferred mechanical method; mowing is not a cut-stump treatment.
Range TN KS-11 lists honeylocust and Osage orange as remove-only pests in Kansas grasslands.

shrubs.name: Roughleaf dogwood, smooth sumac, buckbrush
advice: KS 314 Table 1: roughleaf dogwood high over 15% (2+ yearly burns only maintain it; soil or repeated foliar herbicide); smooth sumac high over 20% (fire increases it; foliar or soil herbicide); buckbrush high over 20% (repeated mowing; 2+ yearly burns control it; repeated foliar or soil herbicide).

KS 528 targeted goats: 8-12 goats per treated acre, at least 80% leaf removal from green-up to end of July in ≤14-day paddock stays, return at half to two-thirds regrowth; browsing after Aug 1 does little; plants over 5 ft need other treatment.
KS 314 PS: after mowing wait at least 2 years before applying herbicide, and wait at least 90 days after herbicide before mowing.
Range TN KS-11 rates these native shrubs remove/reduce/manipulate, depending on whether they are actively encroaching.

shrubs.name: Sand (Chickasaw) plum
advice: KS 314 Table 1: over 20% canopy is high, 10-20% medium; mowing reduces it, fire reduces it and controls it with 2+ yearly burns; foliar or soil herbicide.
Range TN KS-11 rates sand plum a native remove/reduce/manipulate shrub; Forestry TN KS-10 rates sandhill plum high for windbreak and wildlife value.

shrubs.name: Siberian elm, Russian olive, saltcedar
advice: KS 314 Table 1: over 15% canopy is high; elm and Russian olive by cut-surface treatment; fire reduces them (olive needs 2+ yearly burns); elm foliar, soil or basal-bark, olive soil, repeated foliar or basal-bark herbicide; no listed method for saltcedar.
Range TN KS-11: all three are introduced remove-only pests in Kansas grasslands.
PM TN KS-26: saltcedar on a site indicates very high soil salinity, as on old oil-field brine scars.

shrubs.name: Small soapweed (yucca) and pricklypear
advice: KS 314 Table 1: yucca over 20% canopy is high, 10-20% medium, soil herbicide only; pricklypear over 20% high, 10-20% medium, reduced by 2+ yearly burns, foliar herbicide.
Range TN KS-11 rates yucca and plains pricklypear native remove/reduce/manipulate species.

gaps: KDOT seeding specifications (Sections 904 and 2103) returned HTTP 403, so no state DOT roadside mixes are included.

Form KS-ECS-6 Cover Crop Design (per-species cover crop rates and dates) and the KS 340/342/512/550 IR seeding forms were not in the downloaded set; KS 340 soil-health species rates are therefore missing.

KS 589 Crosswind Trap Strips documents (CPS, PS, IR, SOW 2018) are in the KS eFOTG list but were not used in this profile; no 650 Windbreak Renovation document is listed. Only CRP CP24 guidance (TG-22) and KS 380 renovation text were used.

Kansas documents give fixed ready-made native mixes only for an Eastern loamy upland example and sandy CREP sites; West/Central loamy, clay, limy, shallow and saline mixes exist only as percent ranges.
No Kansas-specific rangeland drought stocking rules were found for central and eastern Kansas; MF3716 applies west of Russell and the 99th meridian.
Current Kansas ecological site descriptions (EDIT) and lesser prairie-chicken grazing guidance were not read; only the archived Choppy Sands range site was used.
No revegetation standard for oil and gas well pads or pipelines was found in KCC rules (only pit closure and grading); KDHE surface-mining reclamation rules were not researched.

The Kansas Forest Service species selection guide PDFs returned 404; only the species list pages were read, so the windbreak species list relies on Forestry TN KS-10 (2007) for zones and windbreak value.
Midwest Cover Crops Council decision tool data for Kansas counties (cover crop dates) was not fetched.
The K-State eUpdate article on emergency tillage redirected and could not be read; MF2206 (2013) was used instead.
The region MLRA symbols were read from the TN KS-PM-31 Appendix B map; they were not checked against SSURGO MLRA symbols in this run.
